edits.old: - **Speckle raises the requirement.** A rough target produces a speckle pattern, a random interference pattern of bright and dark spots. A single-mode receiver samples one speckle, whose power is exponentially distributed (Rayleigh-distributed amplitude), so the return sometimes fades deeply. For a detection probability $P_d=0.9$ at a false-alarm probability $P_{\rm fa}=10^{-6}$, one look needs a mean of about **130 detected photons**. This assumes shot-noise-limited coherent detection: the local oscillator's shot noise dominates and thermal and dark-current noise are neglected, which at 105–125 °C holds only approximately (§C4c gives 82–94% of the shot-noise limit for Ge at 125 °C). With the detection threshold $\gamma_{\rm th}$ expressed in units of the mean noise power, and $\bar n$ the mean number of detected signal photons, $P_{\rm fa}=e^{-\gamma_{\rm th}}$ and $P_d=e^{-\gamma_{\rm th}/(1+\bar n)}$, the single-speckle detection law of Eq. (38) (§C0 subsection 10.3) with $p=P_{\rm fa}$. Hence $\bar n=\ln P_{\rm fa}/\ln P_d-1=13.8/0.105-1\approx130$, using $-\ln10^{-6}=13.8$ and $-\ln0.9=0.105$.

edits.finding: §E11.1 Huang et al. and BEV fusion: by analogy
edits.old: - *Fusion* means combining modalities inside one network. *Early fusion* merges raw or low-level data before most processing. *Late fusion*, in Huang et al.'s sense (below), runs a separate *encoder* (the sub-network that turns raw input into features) for each modality and merges their high-level features near the output; §E10.1 calls this merging of learned features *mid fusion*. *BEV fusion* converts each modality into features on a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid, a top-down map of the ground around the car, and merges them there; it too merges learned features, so it is mid fusion in §E10.1's terms. Merging the finished object lists of two separate stacks, as an independent safety channel does (§E10.1, role 3), is a different scheme and is not what "late fusion" means here.

Huang et al.'s theorem is proved for their late-fusion networks, in which the merged features feed the output directly; it carries over to BEV fusion, which processes the merged features further, only by analogy, and §E11.1 checks the effect empirically for camera–lidar detectors. Merging the finished object lists of two separate stacks, as an independent safety channel does (§E10.1, role 3), is a different scheme and is not what "late fusion" means here.

Each channel digitizes 100–400 MHz of beat signal, using the beat-frequency relation $f_b=2BR/(cT)$ of Eq. (85) (§C7; §C0 subsection 2), where $f_b$ is the beat frequency from range alone, $B$ the chirp bandwidth (Hz), $T$ the chirp duration (s), $R$ the range and $c$ the speed of light. A radial velocity of ±50 m/s adds up to 65 MHz of Doppler shift ($2v_r/\lambda$ with radial velocity $v_r$ and wavelength $\lambda\approx1.55$ µm). In the §C7a central 2026 model one channel's four receivers draw ≈0.18 W ($E_{\rm rx}/T_{\rm dwell}=2.34\ \mu{\rm J}/12.67\ \mu{\rm s}$). After the 3 W overhead a 10–15 W sensor therefore holds ≈38–65 channels even if its light were free ($(10-3)/0.184$ to $(15-3)/0.184$), i.e. 3.0–5.1 Mpts/s, and supports only 1.4–2.4 Mpts/s once the light is paid for ($7\ {\rm W}/4.90\ \mu{\rm J}$ to $12\ {\rm W}/4.90\ \mu{\rm J}$) [E].
